objectives.label: Basic circle terms and radii
objectives.description: Identify and use the basic terms of the circle (centre, radius, chord, diameter, surface of the circle, points inside, on and outside) and use radii and diameters to compare lengths and solve problems.

objectives.label: Axes of symmetry in circle
objectives.description: Describe the axes of symmetry of a circle and state that any straight line through the centre is an axis of symmetry.

objectives.label: Chord–centre perpendicular corollaries
objectives.description: Apply the corollaries relating the centre, a chord and its midpoint or perpendicular to calculate lengths, angles and areas and to prove statements about chords.

passages.text: Yousef used the program, Google Earth, on his computer to study the geography of Egypt. Yousef noticed some green, circular areas next to the desert areas so, he asked his father about them.

A.why: Yousef sees green circular fields on Google Earth, a picturable situation motivating circles.

B.why: Yousef sees green circles on Google Earth, which opens the lesson as a whole.

passages.text: The father Said: You learn that a drop of water means the source of life. Therefore, we should minimize the consumption of water in order to irrigate the land by the central irrigation method (sprinkle irrigation) in which, the wheels of the irrigation machine circle around a fixex point which draws those circles.

A.why: Pivot irrigation machines circle round a fixed point and draw circles in the fields.

B.why: Central-pivot irrigation draws circles in the land, a situation a student can picture, and it sets up the lesson.

passages.text: When drawing circle M in a plane, it divides the points of the plane in to three sets of points as in the figure, and they are :

A.why: Introduces what a circle does: it splits the plane into points inside, on and outside.

B.why: It introduces what a circle does to the points of the plane: three sets, inside, on and outside.

passages.text: In the figure opposite $\overline{MA}$, $\overline{MB}$, $\overline{MC}$ are radii for circle M where: MA = MB = MC = radius length of the circle (r)

A.why: A definition note restating that radii of a circle are equal.

B.why: It states a fact about radii in a figure and gives no motivation.

passages.text: From the previous activity we deduce that :

A.why: A transition phrase leading to a stated conclusion, no content itself.

B.why: It is a short lead-in to a deduction with no content of its own.

passages.text: What is the number of axes of symmetry in the circle?

A.why: Asks the student to work out the number of axes of symmetry, not a reflection.

B.why: It asks the student to find the number of axes of symmetry, which is a question to work out.

passages.text: Construction: Draw $\overline{ME} \perp \overline{AB}$ to intersect it at E.

A.why: A construction step of a proof.

B.why: It is a construction step in a proof.

passages.text: Proof: In the larger circle $\overleftrightarrow{ME} \perp \overline{AB}$, so $EA = EB$ (1) (corollary). In the smaller circle $\overleftrightarrow{ME} \perp \overline{CD}$, so $EC = ED$ (2) (corollary). By subtracting (2) from (1), we get: $EA - EC = EB - ED$, so $\therefore AC = BD$ (Q.E.D.)

A.why: A worked proof.

B.why: It is a step of a worked proof.

passages.text: If $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$ are two parallel chords in a circle where $AB > CD$, which chord is closer to the center of the circle? Explain your answer.

A.why: Asks the student to work out and explain which chord is closer, a task not a reflection.

B.why: It asks the student to work out and explain which chord is closer, so it is a reasoning task, not a reflection.

lessons.title: Positions of a point, a Straight Line and a Circle with Respect to a Circle

objectives.label: Position of a point relative to a circle
objectives.description: Determine the position of a point with respect to a circle by comparing MA with the radius r, and find unknown values (x) from such conditions.

objectives.label: Line and circle; tangents
objectives.description: Determine whether a straight line is outside, a secant or a tangent to a circle by comparing the distance MA with the radius r, and use the perpendicularity of a tangent to the radius at the point of tangency to calculate lengths and angles and to justify that a line is a tangent.

objectives.label: Position of two circles
objectives.description: Determine the position of two circles (distant, touching externally or internally, intersecting, concentric) by comparing MN with r_1 + r_2 and r_1 - r_2.

objectives.label: Line of centers applications
objectives.description: Use the line of centers of touching or intersecting circles, with the common tangent and the common chord, to calculate lengths and angles and to prove relations.

passages.text: In the figure opposite, circle M divides the points of the plane in to three sets of points.

A.why: The book introduces that a circle divides the plane's points into three sets, setting up the position of a point.

B.why: It says a circle divides the plane into three sets of points, which introduces the idea of a point's position relative to a circle.

passages.text: If M circle with radius length r and A was a point on the circle plane, then:

A.why: It restates the rule for a point's position by comparing MA with r, with no motivating idea.

B.why: It restates the setup for comparing MA with r, which is a formal statement.

passages.text: If M circle with radius length of r, L is a straight line on its plane, $\overleftrightarrow{MA} \perp L$ where $\overleftrightarrow{MA} \cap L = \{A\}$, Then:

A.why: It sets up a theorem or rule statement for a line and a circle, a formula-style restatement.

B.why: It sets up the line-and-circle statement with symbols and no real motivation.

passages.text: In each of the following cases, Find $L \cap$ surface of circle M.

A.why: It asks the student to work out an intersection, which is a task and not an introduction.

B.why: It asks the student to find an intersection, which is a task.

passages.text: How many tangents can be drawn to circle M ? First: from a point on the circle. Second: from a point outside the circle.

A.why: It asks the student to find how many tangents can be drawn, which is work to do.

B.why: It asks the student to count tangents, which is a work-it-out prompt.

passages.text: What is the relation between the two drawn tangents to the circle from the two end points of any diameter in it ?

A.why: It asks the student to find a relation, which is work to do and not a look back.

B.why: It asks the student to work out a relation between tangents, so it is a task, not a reflection or intro.

objectives.label: Circle through one point
objectives.description: Draw circles passing through a given point, choosing centers and using the compass, and state that infinitely many such circles exist (equal radii give centers on a congruent circle centered at A).

objectives.label: Circle through two points
objectives.description: Draw circles passing through two given points using the axis of the chord AB for the center, and determine the possible circles for a given radius or diameter, including the smallest radius.

objectives.label: Circle through three points
objectives.description: Draw the circumcircle through three noncollinear points as the intersection of the axes of two sides, identify its center in the triangle, and explain why collinear points give no circle.

passages.text: A circle can be drawn (identified) with given terms:

A.why: The book introduces what it means to identify a circle from given terms, opening the whole lesson.

B.why: Opens the lesson by saying a circle can be identified by given conditions, with no worked numbers.

passages.text: Given: A is a given point on the plane. R.T.P: Draw a circle passing through point A. Construction:

A.why: It is the given/required/construction setup for a drawing, not a motivating idea.

B.why: A 'Given / R.T.P' statement that starts a construction.

passages.text: What are the number of points on the plane? What are the number of circles that can be drawn and pass through point A ?

A.why: It asks the student to work out the number of points and circles, so it is a working question.

B.why: Asks the student to count points and circles, which is a work-out question.

passages.text: If the radii of these circles are equal in length, where are their centers located ?

A.why: It asks the student to find where the centers lie, which is a working question.

B.why: Asks the student to find where the centers lie, which is a work-out question.

passages.text: Given: A and B are two given points in the plane. R.T.P: Draw circle M passing through the two points A and B i.e AB is a chord in circle M.

A.why: It is a given/required statement for the construction, not a motivating idea.

B.why: A 'Given / R.T.P' statement of a construction.

passages.text: What is the number of points of the straight line L? What is the number of circles that can be drawn andpass through the two points A and B ?

A.why: It asks the student to count points and circles, which is a working question.

B.why: Asks the student to count points and circles, which is a work-out question.

passages.text: What is the radius length of the smallest circle that can be drawn to pass through the two points A and B ?

A.why: It asks the student to compute the smallest radius, which is a working question.

B.why: Asks the student to find the smallest radius, which is a calculation task.

passages.text: Can two circles intersect at more than two points ?

A.why: It asks the student to decide a fact about circle intersections, which is a working question.

B.why: A question the student must work out, not a reflection after the work.

passages.text: Given: A, B and C are three given points on the plane. R.T.P: Draw circle M passing through the three points A, B and C.

A.why: It is a given/required statement for the construction, not a motivating idea.

B.why: A 'Given / R.T.P' statement of a construction, not a motivating situation.

lessons.title: The Relation Between the Chords of a Circle and its Center

objectives.label: Chord length versus distance
objectives.description: Compare the lengths of chords of a circle with their distances from the center, using >, < and =, and find the range of a value from such a comparison.

objectives.label: Equal chords are equidistant
objectives.description: Use the theorem that equal chords are equidistant from the center (also in congruent circles) to find lengths and angles and to prove equalities.

objectives.label: Converse: equidistant chords are equal
objectives.description: Use the converse of the theorem, that chords equidistant from the center(s) are equal in length, to calculate chord lengths and prove chords equal, including in concentric and intersecting circles.

passages.text: In the figure opposite: A is a point on circle M the chords AB, AC, AD, AE, AF were inscribed in it.

A.why: It only describes a figure with chords drawn from a point A.

B.why: It describes a figure with chords drawn from a point and has no why or what idea.

passages.text: Notice that: The distance of chord AE from the center of circle M equals MX where X is the midpoint of the chord AE, in circle M which its radius length is r.

A.why: It is a side note defining the distance of a chord from the center.

B.why: It is a side note that defines the distance of a chord from the center.

passages.text: Given: $AB = CD$, $\overline{MX} \perp \overline{AB}$, $\overline{MY} \perp \overline{CD}$. R.T.P.: Prove that $MX = MY$. Construction: Draw $\overline{MA}$, $\overline{MC}$.

A.why: It sets out the given, the required proof and the construction for a proof.

B.why: It gives the given, the required proof and the construction for the proof, which are setup steps.

passages.text: Proof: ∵ $\overline{MX}\perp\overline{AB}$ ∴ $AX=\frac{1}{2}AB$. ∵ $\overline{MY}\perp\overline{CD}$ ∴ $CY=\frac{1}{2}CD$. ∵ $AB=CD$ ∴ $AX=CY$. ∵ the two triangles AXM and CYM both have: $AM=CM$; $m(\angle AXM)=m(\angle CYM)=90^\circ$; $AX=CY$ (Proof). ∴ $\triangle AXM \equiv \triangle CYM$. We get: $MX=MY$ (Q.E.D.)

A.why: It is a worked proof of the theorem.

B.why: It is the worked proof, a step-by-step solution.

passages.text: In the figure opposite: The two circles M and N are congruent, $AB = CD$, $\overline{MX}\perp\overline{AB}$, $\overline{NY}\perp\overline{CD}$, then: $MX = NY$.

A.why: It restates the theorem for congruent circles as an example.

B.why: It states a figure and a result for two congruent circles, which is a theorem restated with no motivating context.

passages.text: If M and N are two congruent circles and intersecting at A and B. Is $\overleftrightarrow{AB}$ an axis to $\overline{MN}$? Explain your answer.

A.why: It asks the student to work out and explain a geometric fact, not to reflect on the lesson.

B.why: It asks the student to work out and justify an answer about intersecting congruent circles, so it is not a motivating context or a reflection.
